Ultra-Rare 1970 Hemi Superbird Never Raced NASCAR, Instead Father and Son Hit 220 MPH in It
26 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
This 1970 Plymouth Hemi Superbird was bought brand new by SCTA veteran Jim Lindsley to conquer the salt instead of NASCAR ovals. One of just 135 ever built, this car shattered the 220 mph barrier at Bonneville in 1975 to become the world’s fastest production car. Raced for 18 years by Jim and his son, the Superbird still retains its original, numbers-matching 426 Hemi engine today.
Back in 1970, Plymouth built the Superbird with a sole purpose: to dominate NASCAR’s high-banked superspeedways. Yet, one of the rarest examples ever to roll off the assembly line never turned a wheel on a paved oval in its life.
Instead, Southern California Timing Association veteran and co-founder of the Gear Grinders club Jim Lindsley purchased a brand-new, Alpine White Plymouth Hemi Superbird from the showroom floor and took it straight to the flats of El Mirage and Bonneville to make history. And history he made.
Right from the get-go, Jim Lindsley had zero intention of using it as a street car. All he wanted to do was see how fast Plymouth’s NASCAR aero warrior could go on salt. And in 1971, the car logged a one-way pass of 206 mph at Bonneville. This achievement made Jim and his son, Larry, the very first father-and-son duo inducted into the prestigious Bonneville 200 MPH Club.
Photo: Mecum Auctions To earn a shot at an official record, a car must first make a single run down the salt that beats the existing class record. So in 1972, the Lindsleys were back at Bonneville. Their Superbird ran 211.76 mph, successfully topping the existing 210.048 mph Class B Production record to qualify.
After proving its speed in 1972, the Lindsleys returned in 1973 and recorded the fastest overall speed in their specific competition category (Class B Production), earning the "First in Class" trophy for that event. And they didn't stop there.
During Speed Week in 1975, father and son broke the 220 mph (322 kph) barrier at Bonneville. That run officially made the 1970 Plymouth Hemi Superbird the fastest production car on Earth at the time, a record that stood for years.
However, the exact SCTA record breaker isn't publicly documented. The SCTA archives don’t pinpoint the exact driver or year that beat the Superbird's 1975 Class B Production mark, though it stood well into the 1980s before newer cars surpassed it.
Photo: Mecum Auctions Plymouth built roughly 1,935 Superbirds for NASCAR homologation in 1970, and only 135 left the factory with the 426 Hemi V8 engine like this car. Of the 135 Hemi-powered cars, only 77 were equipped with the automatic transmission like this one, which makes it extremely rare.
The Lindsleys raced the Superbird for its first two seasons using the factory Hemi, rated at 425 horsepower (431 metric horsepower) and 490 pound-feet (664 Newton meters) of torque. Plymouth did not publish an official factory top speed; road tests and gearing calculations with the standard 3.55:1 rear axle place stock top speed right around 144 mph (232 kph) at redline.
Every 426 Hemi Superbird with an auto box came standard with the A36 Performance Axle Package featuring a 3.55:1 Sure-Grip differential. While its aerodynamic body could exceed 200 mph in NASCAR trim, the factory street gearing capped its top speed below 150 mph (241 kph).
The father and the son eventually realized how rare their car was and were afraid they might ruin it. So, in order to push it to its limits, yet protect its rarity, they pulled the Hemi V8 out and placed it into climate-controlled storage.
Photo: Mecum Auctions Jim and his son, Larry, campaigned the 1970 Plymouth superbird at both El Mirage dry lake and the Bonneville Salt Flats from 1970 through 1988, running various race-prepped configurations for further record attempts.
The original 426 Hemi engine wasn’t reunited with the chassis until 2000, during the 1970 Plymouth Superbird’s first restoration. Now it features proper dual Carter AFB four-barrel carburetors and is mated to a correct 1970 Hemi-spec A727 TorqueFlite three-speed automatic transmission.
Because the Superbird ran in the SCTA Production classes, rules required the factory interior, including the original black dashboard, door panels, and trim, to remain intact. However, the chassis still wears physical evidence of engineering that took it to over 220 mph (322 kph).
For instance, the rear tail lamp panel retains the original access holes drilled for the stopping parachute cables. The passenger-side front fender still features holes from an experimental period fuel-cell installation used to balance front-end downforce at extreme speeds.
Photo: Mecum Auctions While the car wore several liveries across its 18-year racing career, it was refinished in 2021 to match its original 1970/1971 Bonneville race look. Today, looking just like it did over half a century ago, the 1970 Plymouth Superbird is scheduled to cross the auction block January 15, 2027, at Mecum’s Kissimmee event in Florida.
The record-breaking aero warrior is going with its original factory broadcast sheet, original pink slip title issued in Jim Lindsley’s name, a set of original Rallye wheels, and an extensive archive of period Bonnevile racing photographs.
